# Two Years On: Follow-up of the Varden County Trial and a Subset of Halden Pilot Organisations

*Field report. A. Lindqvist, P. Mahony, D. Rao (Varden County Evaluation Unit / Easterly University) and R. Okafor (Halden Institute for Work Studies). Registered follow-up protocol VC-2023-04-F, filed at month 11.*

## Summary

We report 24-month outcomes from two sources: the Varden County cluster-randomised trial, whose case-processing offices remained on their assigned schedules for two years, and 14 organisations from the Halden pilot that hold record-based output data. In Varden case-processing offices, the gain in output per actual hour relative to control fell from 12.5% at nine months to 8.5% at 24 months, measured with system log data, and output per employee stood at −3.4% (95% CI −8.0 to +1.2). The gain has therefore declined but not disappeared. A registered mediation test confirms that the reduction in recurring meetings accounts for 47% (95% CI 28 to 66%) of the per-hour gain; improved fatigue accounts for 18% (2 to 34%). The counter and contact-centre arm was ended by the county at month 12 because of waiting times. Three of the 14 Halden organisations have reverted, all with client-facing or coverage obligations.

## 1. Background

The nine-month report of the Varden trial left three questions to be settled at follow-up: whether the per-hour gain in case-processing would persist; whether the meetings association, found in an unregistered analysis, would survive a registered test; and whether timesheets understated the work actually done. Two subsequent publications bear on the first two. A re-analysis of the Halden pilot argued that per-hour gains in reduced-hours schemes are entirely an artifact of measurement, selection and novelty, and that the meetings hypothesis was a post hoc story. A meta-analysis of 23 studies concluded that effects show no sign of decay, on the basis of four studies with follow-up beyond 12 months. We address each directly.

## 2. Varden County: design at 24 months

The seven treated and seven control case-processing offices kept their assigned schedules for 24 months. To address concern about unrecorded work, we added a second hours measure: active log-in time on the county's case-management system, which records time staff are working on cases whether or not they claim it on a timesheet. The mediation analysis was registered at month 11, before 24-month outcomes were available. It specified two mediators, weekly hours in recurring meetings (from calendar data) and a validated fatigue scale, and a single outcome, output per log-measured hour.

The counter and contact-centre arm was ended by the county at month 12. In months 10 to 12, average waiting time in treated counter offices was 7.3 minutes against 4.0 in control offices, and the county judged that restoring service would require 12% more staff, raising the cost per contact handled by an estimated 9%. Those offices returned to 37.5 hours.

## 3. Varden County: results

**Table 1. Case-processing offices, treated relative to control (difference-in-differences)**

| Outcome | 9 months | 24 months |
|---|---|---|
| Output per FTE | −2.1% (−6.8 to +2.6) | −3.4% (−8.0 to +1.2) |
| Actual hours, timesheets | −13% | −12% |
| Actual hours, system logs | — | −11% |
| Output per hour, timesheets | +12.5% (+6.9 to +18.4) | +9.8% (+4.6 to +15.2) |
| Output per hour, system logs | — | +8.5% (+3.4 to +13.8) |
| Appeal overturn rate (treated v control) | 3.1% v 3.0% | 3.2% v 3.0% |
| Sick days per FTE | −29% | −27% |
| Annual resignations (treated v control) | 3.9% v 7.4% | 4.1% v 7.9% |

Log data show slightly more work than timesheets: actual hours fell by 11% on logs and 12% on timesheets, so the per-hour gain on the stricter measure is 8.5%. That gain is smaller than at nine months but its confidence interval excludes zero by a clear margin. Output per employee remains slightly below control; the hours reduction is mostly, not fully, offset.

The decline from 12.5% to 9.8% on the like-for-like timesheet measure is consistent with some fading of an initial effect. It is not consistent with the gain falling to zero by month ten, as an extrapolation of self-reported energy in the Halden data had suggested.

### Mediation

Recurring meeting time in treated case-processing offices fell from 7.4 to 3.9 hours per week per person between baseline and month 24; in control offices it moved from 7.2 to 7.0. Fatigue scores improved by 0.34 standard deviations in treated offices relative to control.

**Table 2. Registered mediation analysis, output per log-measured hour, 24 months**

| Pathway | Share of per-hour gain explained (95% CI) |
|---|---|
| Reduction in recurring meetings | 47% (28 to 66) |
| Improvement in fatigue | 18% (2 to 34) |
| Unexplained | 35% |

The meetings pathway, first suggested in the nine-month report's exploratory analysis and since dismissed as post hoc, survives a registered test with a larger sample of office-months and a pre-specified model. Reduced fatigue contributes, but less than half as much. About a third of the gain is not explained by either measured pathway.

### An unplanned observation

In month 15, two control offices, on their own initiative and without changing hours, carried out a "meeting audit" and cancelled a number of standing meetings. Recurring meeting time in those two offices fell from 7.1 to 5.0 hours per week, and their output per hour over the following six months was 4.1% above their own previous six months. This is two offices, uncontrolled, and the change was smaller than in treated offices. It suggests, without establishing, that part of the per-hour gain might be available without reducing hours. Whether reorganisation alone could capture most of the gain, or whether the hours cut is what makes such reorganisation happen and stick, cannot be determined from this trial, since no arm reorganised without reducing hours.

## 4. Halden organisations at 24 months

We contacted the 23 Halden organisations that had submitted output records; 14 agreed to provide 24-month data. Three of these had reverted to a five-day schedule: a hospitality group and a retail chain, both citing coverage of opening hours, and a marketing agency citing client deadlines. Their record-based output indices at the time of reversion were between 88 and 91.

Among the 11 that continued, record-based output at 24 months stood at 96.8 against the pre-pilot baseline, and actual hours from time tracking at 34.9 against 40.3 (−13.4%), an implied gain in output per actual hour of 11.8%. These organisations have no comparison group and are survivors twice over: they completed the pilot and then chose to continue. Their figures are an upper bound for organisations that self-select into reduced hours and find it suits them, not an estimate for organisations in general.

## 5. Bearing on earlier claims

**The re-analysis's claim that per-hour gains are entirely an artifact.** The Varden 24-month estimate uses record-based output, log-measured hours, randomised comparison and a two-year horizon, the standards that re-analysis itself recommended, and finds a gain of 8.5% (3.4 to 13.8). The re-analysis was right about the measurement problems it identified and right that headline figures were inflated; its conclusion that nothing remains once those problems are corrected is not supported.

**The meta-analysis's claim that effects show no sign of decay.** The four studies with follow-up beyond 12 months, listed in the meta-analysis's supplementary table, were all uncontrolled and all used scheduled hours. Their pooled estimate therefore reflects the design features the meta-analysis itself found to inflate effects, and it cannot speak to decay. In the one controlled study with long follow-up, this one, the per-hour gain declined by about a quarter between nine and 24 months.

## 6. Limitations

One public employer; seven offices per arm in the case-processing stratum. Mediation analysis assumes no unmeasured confounding between mediators and outcome, which a cluster trial cannot guarantee. The Halden subset is small and self-selected. Neither source extends beyond 24 months.

</document>
response:
# A Close Reading of the Two-Year Follow-up

**The report's claim.** In Varden's case-processing offices, the per-hour gain shrank between nine and 24 months but did not disappear. On the stricter log-based hours measure it is 8.5%, with an interval clearly above zero. A registered mediation test attributes about half the gain to fewer meetings and less than a fifth to reduced fatigue. The counter arm was stopped because of waiting times. In the Halden subset, survivors kept a gain of about 12%, and three more organisations reverted.

This is a strong follow-up. It does what the nine-month report promised:

- it adds a log-based hours measure to check timesheets;
- it registers the mediation test before the outcomes were available;
- it answers both Varga & Holm and the meta-analysis with the kind of evidence each called for.

Section 5's point about the meta-analysis is decisive: the four long-follow-up studies were all uncontrolled and used scheduled hours. That confirms the confounding suspected in the meta-analysis's duration claim.

The arithmetic holds:

- 0.966 / 0.88 → +9.8%; 0.966 / 0.89 → +8.5%.
- Halden: 34.9 / 40.3 → −13.4%, and 96.8 / 86.6 → +11.8%.
- Mediation shares: 47 + 18 + 35 = 100.

The remaining issues are mostly about wording and a few gaps, but two of them matter for the mediation claim.

## 1. The Summary compares different measures

"Fell from 12.5% at nine months to 8.5% at 24 months" compares a **timesheet** figure with a **log** figure. On the same measure, the change is 12.5% → 9.8%, about a 22% decline, which is what the body correctly reports. The Summary overstates the decline. That is a conservative error, but the paper should be internally consistent.

The decline itself is also not tested. The two intervals (6.9–18.4 and 4.6–15.2) overlap heavily. "Consistent with some fading" is fair. "Declined by about a quarter", as in §5, states as a finding something the data only suggest.

## 2. "Confirms" overstates the mediation result

The body says the meetings pathway "survives a registered test", which is accurate. The Summary says the test "confirms" that meetings account for 47%. Three reasons to keep the softer wording:

- **The mediator was not randomised.** Mediation relies on sequential ignorability. The limitations section concedes this, but the Summary doesn't. Offices whose managers cut meetings may differ in management quality, which could drive both fewer meetings and more output per hour.
- **The test uses the same units as the original hypothesis.** It was registered at month 11, after the nine-month exploratory result, in the same seven treated offices. That makes it a pre-specified test, which is a real improvement, but not an independent replication. Varga & Holm's worry about a model "fitted to a subgroup" is narrowed, not eliminated.
- **The "larger sample of office-months" is not a larger sample.** The effective sample is still 7 v 7 clusters, because repeated months in the same office are not independent. The paper should state how the mediation intervals account for clustering. If they treat office-months as independent, 28–66% is too narrow.

There is also an accounting point. Meeting time is part of hours worked. If output is produced mainly outside meetings, cutting meetings raises output per hour almost by definition. Part of the "mediation" may therefore be composition rather than behaviour change. The policy implication is the same, but the 47% is not purely a causal pathway in the usual sense. Reporting output per non-meeting hour would separate the two.

## 3. The control arm was contaminated

The two control offices that ran a "meeting audit" in month 15 are an interesting observation, and the report treats them cautiously. But they also **contaminate the control arm**. If control output per hour rose from month 15, the 24-month difference-in-differences is biased downward. The obvious sensitivity check is missing: the 24-month estimate excluding those two offices, or excluding months 15–24 for them.

Control staff knew about the trial, and the meetings finding had been circulated. The audit may itself have been a response to the trial. That doesn't change the conclusion, but it should be stated.

## 4. A Halden reversion doesn't fit the stated pattern

The Summary says all three reversions had "client-facing or coverage obligations". One was a **marketing agency citing client deadlines**. That is deadline-bound discretionary work, not coverage-bound work in the meta-analysis's sense. Folding it into "coverage" makes the pattern look cleaner than it is.

This is the first reversion in the Halden data outside retail and healthcare administration. One case is not a trend, but it should be reported as an exception, not absorbed.

## 5. The Halden hours baseline may be borrowed

The 11 continuing organisations' hours are compared with a baseline of **40.3**. That is the baseline Varga & Holm reported for the 27 organisations with time tracking, not necessarily the baseline for these 11. If the 11 have their own baseline, it should be used. If 40.3 is coincidentally theirs too, say so. Otherwise the 11.8% rests on a mismatched denominator.

Selection is also deeper than "survivors twice over". These organisations:

1. completed the pilot;
2. had submitted records;
3. agreed to provide follow-up data, with 9 of 23 declining;
4. chose to continue.

The report's "upper bound" framing is right, but the chain is longer than stated.

## 6. Questions still open from earlier rounds

- **Backlog and deadline compliance.** The nine-month report itself raised whether backlogs might exceed statutory deadlines. With output per FTE at −3.4% for two years and intake presumably unchanged, the queue grows. Neither backlog size nor deadline compliance is reported, and it is the obvious cost of a small per-employee shortfall in backlog work.
- **Sick days.** The −27% still isn't expressed per scheduled day or hour. Without knowing how the 30 hours were arranged, part of it may be the mechanical effect of fewer working days.
- **Quality and resignations.** Neither has confidence intervals. Overturn rates of 3.2% v 3.0% are more informative at 24 months, since appeals have had time to resolve, but they still need intervals.
- **Halden attrition.** A Halden author co-signs this report, and it does not address the misreported timing and reasons for the nine withdrawals that Varga & Holm documented. This is the natural place to correct the record.

## 7. Counter-arm costing

The +9% cost per contact from 12% more staff is plausible, but its derivation isn't shown. Showing it matters, because this is the figure a county board would act on.

## Where the evidence now stands

| Question | Current answer | Strength |
|---|---|---|
| Per-hour gain, discretionary/backlog work | About 8–10% at 24 months (Varden, randomised, log hours); about 12% in Halden survivors (upper bound) | Moderate: one employer, 7 v 7 offices |
| Durability | Partial fading (12.5% → 9.8% like-for-like), not to zero | Weak to moderate: decline not tested |
| Per worker, discretionary work | Slightly below control (−2% to −3%), interval includes 0 | Moderate |
| Per worker, coverage-bound work | Clear loss; service worse; restoring it costs about 9% more per contact | Moderate to strong |
| Mechanism | Fewer meetings is the leading candidate (about half); fatigue smaller; a third unexplained | Suggestive: pre-specified but same units, unrandomised mediator |
| Gain without cutting hours | Two control offices hint yes; untested | Anecdotal |

Each earlier document overstated in one direction:

- **Halden:** gains are large and sector-general.
- **Varga & Holm:** gains are entirely artifact.
- **The meta-analysis:** no decay, so novelty can be set aside.

This report corrects all three with better evidence. Its own overstatements are smaller: "confirms" for mediation, a cross-measure comparison in the Summary, and a reversion stretched to fit a category.

The most useful next study follows from the report's own last line: a trial with an arm that **reorganises meetings without cutting hours**. That would show whether the hours cut is the cause or just what triggers the reorganisation.

I can draft referee comments, a reply to the report on behalf of the meta-analysis authors, or a one-page synthesis of all five documents if useful.
